goals: Relate the nitrogenous waste of an animal to its habitat

slides.heading: Excretory Products and Their Elimination
slides.body_md: Part 1: nitrogenous wastes, the kidney and the formation of urine.

nodes.label: Urine to the bladder and out

visual.alt: Flow from nitrogenous waste to urine

slides.narration: Cells break down proteins and nucleic acids, and the nitrogen in them has to leave the body. Animals do this in different ways, and in humans the kidneys do the main work. This part covers the kinds of waste, the structure of the kidney and nephron, and the way urine is made.

slides.heading: Ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism
slides.body_md: Most animals excrete nitrogen as **ammonia, urea or uric acid**, depending on how much water they can spare.

rows: Most toxic; a lot of water
Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects
Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes

visual.alt: Table of the three modes of excretion with waste, toxicity and examples

slides.narration: Ammonia is very toxic and needs a great deal of water to flush it out, so it suits animals that live in water. Urea is less toxic and is made in the liver. Uric acid is almost insoluble, and animals that must save water, such as birds and reptiles, pass it out as a paste.

slides.narration: Quick check. Think of an embryo sealed inside a shell.

slides.heading: Excretory structures in animals
slides.body_md: Different animals use different structures to collect and remove wastes.

visual.alt: Table of excretory structures in animals

slides.narration: Flame cells of flatworms, nephridia of earthworms, Malpighian tubules of insects, green glands of prawns and kidneys of vertebrates all collect wastes and regulate water, but they differ in structure. In humans the kidneys are the main excretory organs.

slides.heading: The human kidney in longitudinal section
slides.body_md: The **kidneys** are a pair of reddish-brown, bean-shaped organs between the last thoracic and the third lumbar vertebra. The **L.S.** shows an outer **cortex** (which dips in as **renal columns**), an inner **medulla** of **renal pyramids**, **calyces**, the **renal pelvis** and the **hilum**.

visual.alt: Labelled longitudinal section of the human kidney

slides.narration: The kidney has a tough capsule. Beneath it is the cortex, which also extends between the cone-shaped pyramids of the medulla as renal columns. The pyramids open into cup-like calyces that join the renal pelvis, which leads to the ureter. The hilum is the notch where vessels and the ureter enter or leave.

slides.heading: The excretory system and the kidney in numbers
slides.body_md: The system has **two kidneys, two ureters, one urinary bladder and one urethra**. Urine passes from the pelvis by the ureter to the bladder and to the outside by the urethra.

rows: About 10 to 12 cm long, 5 to 7 cm wide, 2 to 3 cm thick
Renal artery in; renal vein out

visual.alt: Table of facts about the kidney

slides.narration: Each kidney holds about a million nephrons, which are its structural and functional units. Blood enters by the renal artery and leaves by the renal vein. Urine collects in the pelvis, passes down the ureter to the bladder, and is released through the urethra.

slides.heading: The nephron and its blood supply
slides.body_md: A nephron has a **Malpighian body** (**glomerulus** + **Bowman’s capsule**) and a **tubule**: **PCT**, **loop of Henle** (descending and ascending limbs), **DCT**, ending in the **collecting duct**. The **afferent arteriole** is wider than the **efferent arteriole**, which gives the **peritubular capillaries** and **vasa recta**.

slides.narration: Blood enters the glomerulus by the wide afferent arteriole and leaves by the narrower efferent arteriole, which builds up pressure. The filtrate passes through the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal tubule and the collecting duct. Blood from the efferent arteriole supplies the capillaries around the tubules.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting nephrons
slides.body_md: Each kidney has about **1,000,000 nephrons**, and about **15 percent** are **juxtamedullary** (long loops of Henle with vasa recta); the rest are **cortical**. Find the numbers in both kidneys.
bullets: Juxtamedullary $= 15/100 \times 2000000 = 300000$.

visual.alt: Worked table of the numbers of nephrons

slides.narration: Two kidneys with a million nephrons each give two million in all. Fifteen percent of these are juxtamedullary, which is three hundred thousand. The remaining one million seven hundred thousand are cortical nephrons with short loops of Henle.

slides.heading: Urine formation: three processes
slides.body_md: Urine is formed by **glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration)**, **selective reabsorption** and **tubular secretion**.

rows: Blood pressure forces water and small solutes (not proteins) through a three-layered membrane
Mainly PCT; also loop, DCT, collecting duct
Glucose, amino acids, salts and water return to the blood
H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia pass from blood into the filtrate

visual.alt: Table of the three processes of urine formation

slides.narration: Filtration forces fluid out of the glomerulus, and only the proteins and blood cells stay behind. The tubules then take back what the body needs, such as glucose and most of the water. Finally the tubule cells add substances like hydrogen ions and potassium to the filtrate.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much filtrate is made
slides.body_md: The **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** of a healthy adult is about **120 mL per minute** (textbooks give about 125). The daily urine is about **1.5 L**. How much filtrate is made in a day, and what share is reabsorbed?
bullets: Filtrate $= 120 \times 1440 / 1000 = 172.8$ L a day.
Share reabsorbed $= 171.3/172.8 \times 100 \approx 99.1$ percent.
The PCT alone takes back about 70 percent: $70/100 \times 172.8 = 121$ L.

visual.alt: Worked table of the daily volumes of filtrate and urine

slides.narration: Multiply the rate by the minutes in a day to find the filtrate. Subtracting the urine gives the volume that returns to the blood, which is more than ninety nine percent. The proximal tubule alone reabsorbs about seventy percent, which shows how large a share of the work it does.

slides.body_md: Work out the daily filtrate from a lower filtration rate.
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply the rate by the number of minutes in a day.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: why filtration needs pressure
slides.body_md: Net filtration pressure = glomerular blood pressure − (capsule pressure + blood osmotic pressure). In a healthy kidney they are **60**, **18** and **32 mm Hg**.
bullets: $18 + 32 = 50$ mm Hg oppose filtration.
Net pressure $= 60 - 50 = 10$ mm Hg (positive: filtration occurs).
The efferent arteriole is **narrower** than the afferent, which keeps the glomerular pressure high.

visual.alt: Worked table of the net filtration pressure

slides.narration: Blood pressure in the glomerulus pushes fluid out, while the pressure in the capsule and the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins push the other way. The balance is a small positive pressure, which is enough for filtration. If the blood pressure falls too far, filtration stops.

slides.heading: The tubule segments and what they do
slides.body_md: Each segment of the tubule has a different permeability and job.

rows: Reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids, and 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water; secretion of H⁺, K⁺, ammonia
Permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes: filtrate becomes concentrated
Impermeable to water; salts leave: filtrate becomes dilute
Conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water; secretion of H⁺, K⁺
Reabsorbs large amounts of water: concentrated urine; lets some urea pass into the medulla

visual.alt: Table of the segments of the tubule and their functions

slides.narration: The proximal tubule does most of the reabsorption. In the loop of Henle the descending limb lets water out, and the ascending limb lets salts out but not water. The distal tubule and collecting duct adjust the water and salt according to what the body needs.

slides.heading: The counter-current mechanism
slides.body_md: Filtrate in the two limbs of the loop of Henle flows in **opposite directions** (counter-current); so does blood in the **vasa recta**. They keep a gradient in the medulla from **300 to 1200 mOsmol per L**, which lets the collecting duct make urine up to **4 times** as concentrated as the filtrate.

decks.title: Excretory Products and Their Elimination — Part 2: regulation, other organs and disorders
goals: Describe how ADH and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system regulate water and salt balance, and the roles of ANF and erythropoietin
Describe micturition and the role of the skin, liver and lungs in excretion

slides.heading: Regulation, other organs and disorders
slides.body_md: Part 2: hormones that control the kidney, excretion by other organs, and kidney failure.

nodes.label: Hormones: ADH, renin, aldosterone, ANF, erythropoietin

visual.alt: Flow of the topics of part two

slides.narration: The kidney does not work alone. Hormones adjust how much water and salt it keeps, and the brain controls the passing of urine. Other organs also remove wastes. This part ends with what goes wrong when the kidneys fail and how dialysis and transplants help.

slides.heading: Regulation by ADH
slides.body_md: When the **osmolarity of body fluids rises** or the volume falls, **osmoreceptors** in the **hypothalamus** make the **neurohypophysis** release **ADH (antidiuretic hormone)**. ADH makes the **distal parts of the tubule** more permeable to water, so **more water is reabsorbed** and less, more concentrated, urine is formed.

nodes.label: DCT and collecting duct reabsorb more water

visual.alt: Flow of the regulation of water balance by ADH

slides.narration: When the body fluid becomes too concentrated, receptors in the hypothalamus signal the release of antidiuretic hormone. The hormone makes the last parts of the tubule take back more water, and the urine is small in volume and concentrated. When enough water has been regained, the release stops.

slides.heading: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
slides.body_md: A fall in **GFR, blood pressure or blood flow** activates the **juxtaglomerular (JG) cells** to release **renin**. Renin converts **angiotensinogen** to **angiotensin I** and then **angiotensin II**, a **vasoconstrictor** that raises the glomerular pressure and the GFR. Angiotensin II also stimulates the **adrenal cortex** to release **aldosterone**, which makes the **DCT** reabsorb **Na⁺ and water**.

nodes.label: Fall in GFR or blood pressure
Angiotensinogen to angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Na⁺ and water retained: pressure and GFR rise

visual.alt: Flow of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

slides.narration: If the blood flow or pressure to the kidney falls, juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renin starts a chain that forms angiotensin two. This narrows blood vessels and also makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone, so that the kidney keeps more sodium and water and the pressure goes back up.

slides.body_md: Predict the effect of a drug that blocks one step.

slides.heading: ANF and erythropoietin
slides.body_md: Several hormones act on or arise from the kidney.

rows: More water reabsorbed; may constrict vessels
Na⁺ and water reabsorbed in DCT
Dilates vessels, lowers pressure; a check on the renin system
More red blood cells made in the bone marrow

visual.alt: Table of hormones that regulate the kidney or arise from it

slides.narration: The atrial natriuretic factor from the heart does the opposite of the renin system: it widens blood vessels and lowers pressure. The kidney itself releases erythropoietin when the oxygen supply is low, which stimulates the bone marrow to make more red blood cells.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: water balance on a hot day
slides.body_md: On a normal day a person takes in **2500 mL** of water and loses **1500** by urine, **600** by skin, **300** by lungs and **100** by faeces. On a hot day sweating raises the skin loss to **1500 mL**. If the intake is the same, how much urine must be formed to keep the balance?
bullets: Normal day: $1500 + 600 + 300 + 100 = 2500$ mL, equal to the intake.
Fall in urine $= (1500 - 600)/1500 \times 100 = 60$ percent; ADH makes this small volume concentrated.

visual.alt: Worked table of water balance on a normal and a hot day

slides.narration: Output must equal intake. On a hot day the skin loses much more water, so the kidney has to form much less urine. More antidiuretic hormone is released, the tubules take back more water, and the small volume of urine is dark and concentrated.

slides.heading: Micturition and urine
slides.body_md: Urine is stored in the **urinary bladder**. When it fills, **stretch receptors** send signals to the **CNS**, which sends back **motor messages**: the **bladder muscle contracts** and the **urethral sphincter relaxes**, so **urine is passed**. An adult can control the sphincter voluntarily.

nodes.label: Motor messages: bladder contracts, sphincter relaxes

visual.alt: Flow of the micturition reflex

slides.narration: The bladder wall has stretch receptors. When it is full, they send signals to the spinal cord and brain. The reply makes the bladder muscle contract and the sphincter relax, and urine leaves through the urethra. A healthy adult passes one to one and a half litres a day, mostly water with urea and salts.

slides.heading: Skin, liver and lungs in excretion
slides.body_md: Besides the kidneys, other organs remove wastes.

rows: Large amounts of CO₂ (about 200 mL a minute) and some water vapour
Bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin), cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs, passed out with the digestive wastes
Sweat with NaCl, small amounts of urea and lactic acid; cools the body
Sebum with sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes; protects and lubricates the skin

visual.alt: Table of the role of the lungs, liver and skin in excretion

slides.narration: The lungs get rid of carbon dioxide and water vapour. The liver sends bile pigments and many other substances into the bile, and they leave with the faeces. The skin removes salts, a little urea and lactic acid in sweat, and the sebaceous glands release oily sebum.

slides.narration: The cellophane tube lets small wastes pass but not blood cells or proteins. Urea leaves the blood by diffusion into the dialysing fluid, because there is none in it. The cleaned blood is returned to the patient through a vein after the heparin has been neutralised.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much does a session clean the blood?
slides.body_md: Before a session a patient’s blood urea is **84 mg per 100 mL**; after it, **28**. The blood flows through the unit at **300 mL per minute** for **4 hours**, three times a week.
bullets: Urea removed $= (84 - 28)/84 \times 100 \approx 66.7$ percent.
Blood passed through the unit $= 300 \times 4 \times 60 / 1000 = 72$ L in one session.
Time on dialysis in a week $= 3 \times 4 = 12$ hours.

visual.alt: Worked table of a dialysis session

slides.narration: Two thirds of the urea is removed in one session, and the level returns towards the upper limit of normal. During the session many times the whole blood volume passes through the unit. Because wastes build up again, the patient needs treatment about three times every week.

slides.heading: Disorders of the excretory system
slides.body_md: Several conditions affect the kidney and urinary tract.

rows: Kidney malfunction lets urea accumulate in the blood
Poisoning of the body; leads to renal failure
Failure of the kidneys to filter blood
Wastes and fluid build up; needs dialysis or a transplant
Insoluble masses of crystallised salts, such as oxalates, form in the kidney
Pain and blockage of the urine flow
Inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney
Protein and blood in the urine; reduced filtration

visual.alt: Table of disorders of the excretory system

slides.narration: When the kidneys stop working properly, urea builds up in the blood, which is called uraemia. Complete failure is dangerous. Stones can form from crystallised salts, and inflammation of the glomeruli, called glomerulonephritis, makes the filter leak and reduces its work.

slides.heading: Dialysis and kidney transplant
slides.body_md: Both treat kidney failure, but in different ways.

rows: Cleans the blood outside the body
A healthy kidney does all the work
About three times a week, for hours each time
Tiring, expensive and a continuing need

visual.alt: Table comparing haemodialysis with kidney transplant

slides.narration: Dialysis replaces only the filtering and has to be repeated. A transplant is the best treatment for permanent failure, because the new kidney does everything. The patient’s immune system may reject it, so doctors prefer a donor with a close tissue match, usually a relative, and give drugs to suppress rejection.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: judging kidney function from clearance
slides.body_md: The GFR can be estimated from **creatinine**, which is filtered but not reabsorbed: **GFR = U × V / P**, where U is its concentration in urine, V the urine flow (mL per minute) and P its concentration in plasma. (This formula is physiology, not syllabus content.) A healthy man: U = 1.5 mg per mL, V = 1.2 mL per minute, P = 0.015 mg per mL.
bullets: $\text{GFR} = 1.5 \times 1.2 / 0.015 = 120$ mL per minute.
A patient: U = 0.9, V = 1, P = 0.018: $\text{GFR} = 0.9 \times 1 / 0.018 = 50$ mL per minute, well below normal.

visual.alt: Worked table of two filtration rates estimated from creatinine

slides.narration: A substance that is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted can be used to measure the filtration rate. The healthy man filters about one hundred and twenty millilitres a minute, but the patient only fifty, which means that his kidneys are working at a fraction of their capacity.

bullets: ADH: more water reabsorbed; renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone: raise pressure and keep Na⁺; ANF lowers pressure; erythropoietin: more red cells.
Micturition: stretch receptors, CNS, bladder contracts, sphincter relaxes.

notes.title: Excretory Products and Their Elimination — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Modes of excretion, the human excretory system, the kidney and the nephron
sections.body_md:
**Nitrogenous wastes.** The breakdown of proteins and nucleic acids releases nitrogen, which is excreted as **ammonia, urea or uric acid**. **Ammonotelism:** ammonia is the most toxic and needs a great deal of water to remove it, so it is the waste of aquatic animals (bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects); it diffuses across body surfaces or gills, and the kidney has little role. **Ureotelism:** urea, less toxic, is made in the **liver** from ammonia and carried in the blood to the kidneys (mammals, many terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes). **Uricotelism:** uric acid, nearly insoluble and least toxic, is passed as a paste with little loss of water (reptiles, birds, land snails, insects). The habitat decides the mode: the more water an animal can spare, the more toxic a waste it can excrete. (Some animals switch with habitat, for example a lungfish in a dry mud burrow makes urea instead of ammonia.)

**Excretory structures.** **Protonephridia (flame cells)** in flatworms, rotifers and Amphioxus; **nephridia** in earthworms; **Malpighian tubules** in insects; **green (antennal) glands** in prawns; **kidneys** in vertebrates.

**The human excretory system** consists of a pair of **kidneys**, a pair of **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and a **urethra**. Each kidney is a reddish-brown, bean-shaped organ, about 10 to 12 cm long, 5 to 7 cm wide and 2 to 3 cm thick, between the last thoracic and the third lumbar vertebra. The notch on the inner concave side is the **hilum**, through which the **ureter, blood vessels and nerves** pass. The **L.S.** shows a tough **capsule**, an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla**. The medulla forms cone-shaped **renal pyramids**, between which the cortex extends as **renal columns**; the pyramids open into **calyces**, which join the funnel-shaped **renal pelvis**.

**The nephron** (the structural and functional unit; nearly one million in each kidney) has the **Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)**, made of the **glomerulus**, a tuft of capillaries fed by the **afferent arteriole** and drained by the narrower **efferent arteriole**, enclosed in the double-walled **Bowman's capsule**; and the **renal tubule**: **proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)** with a brush-border epithelium, the **loop of Henle** (a descending and an ascending limb), the **distal convoluted tubule (DCT)**, which opens into the **collecting duct**. The efferent arteriole forms the **peritubular capillaries** and, in juxtamedullary nephrons, the **vasa recta**. About **85 percent** are **cortical nephrons** (short loops, little or no vasa recta) and about **15 percent** are **juxtamedullary** (long loops reaching deep into the medulla, with vasa recta). So the two kidneys have about 2,000,000 nephrons.

sections.heading: 2. Urine formation and the counter-current mechanism
sections.body_md:
Urine is formed in three steps.

**Ultrafiltration (glomerular filtration).** The blood pressure in the glomerulus, kept high because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent, forces water and small solutes through a **three-layered filtration membrane** (the endothelium of the glomerular capillaries, the epithelium of the Bowman's capsule with its podocytes, and the basement membrane between them). Almost everything except **proteins and blood cells** passes, which is why it is called **ultrafiltration**. About **1100 to 1200 mL of blood** flows through the kidneys each minute, about one fifth of the cardiac output. The **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** is about **125 mL per minute**, or about **180 L a day** (this chapter uses 120 mL per minute, or 172.8 L a day, in its sums). The GFR is regulated by the juxtaglomerular apparatus; a person passes only about 1.5 L of urine a day, so more than 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

**Selective reabsorption.** The **PCT** (simple cuboidal epithelium with a brush border) reabsorbs nearly all the **glucose and amino acids** and about 70 to 80 percent of the **electrolytes and water**, by **active** transport (glucose, amino acids, Na⁺) and **passive** transport (nitrogenous wastes). The **DCT** reabsorbs Na⁺ and water conditionally, and the **collecting duct** reabsorbs large amounts of water.

**Tubular secretion.** The tubule cells add **H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia** to the filtrate (in the PCT and DCT), which helps to maintain the **pH and the ionic balance** of the blood.

**Concentration of urine (counter-current mechanism).** The two limbs of the loop of Henle, and the two limbs of the vasa recta, carry fluid in **opposite directions** (counter-current) and lie close together. The **descending limb** is **permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes**, so water leaves and the filtrate becomes **more concentrated** as it goes down. The **ascending limb** is **impermeable to water** but lets electrolytes out, so the filtrate becomes **dilute** as it goes up. The NaCl leaving the ascending limb is picked up by the descending vasa recta and returned by the ascending vasa recta; urea moves similarly. These exchanges maintain a **gradient in the osmolarity of the medullary tissue fluid from about 300 mOsmol per L in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmol per L in the inner medulla**. The collecting duct passes through this gradient and loses water, so a human can produce urine up to about **4 times as concentrated** as the initial filtrate. The abbreviations to learn are GFR, ADH and ANF.

sections.heading: 3. Regulation of kidney function, erythropoietin, micturition and homeostasis
sections.body_md:
**ADH.** Osmoreceptors in the **hypothalamus** respond to a rise in the osmolarity of body fluids (or fall in volume) and make the **neurohypophysis** release **ADH (antidiuretic hormone)**. ADH facilitates **water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule**, preventing **diuresis**; it can also constrict blood vessels and raise the pressure. When the fluid volume rises, the osmoreceptors are switched off and the release stops (a feedback).

**Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).** The **juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)** is made of the **JG cells** (modified cells of the afferent arteriole) and the **macula densa** (cells of the DCT). A fall in the glomerular blood pressure, blood flow or GFR activates the JG cells to release **renin**, which converts **angiotensinogen** in the blood to **angiotensin I** and then to **angiotensin II**. Angiotensin II is a powerful **vasoconstrictor**, which increases the glomerular blood pressure and the GFR; it also activates the **adrenal cortex** to release **aldosterone**, which causes reabsorption of **Na⁺ and water** from the DCT, raising the blood pressure and the GFR.

**ANF (atrial natriuretic factor).** The atrial walls of the heart release ANF when the blood volume and pressure rise; it causes **vasodilation** and a fall in the blood pressure, and so acts as a **check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism**.

**Erythropoietin.** The kidney (the juxtaglomerular cells) secretes the hormone **erythropoietin** when oxygen is short; it stimulates the **bone marrow to make more red blood cells**. (Books differ on the exact cells; the syllabus asks only for the hormone, its source and its action.)

**Micturition.** Urine is stored in the **urinary bladder** and its release is the **micturition reflex**. When the bladder fills, **stretch receptors** in its wall send signals to the **CNS**, which sends motor messages that make the **bladder muscle contract** and the **urethral sphincter relax**, and urine is voided. The sphincter is under voluntary control in adults. A healthy adult forms about 1 to 1.5 L of urine a day (pH about 6.0) with about 25 to 30 g of urea.

**Homeostasis.** The kidneys regulate the **volume and osmolarity** of body fluids, the **ionic composition**, the **pH** and the **blood pressure**, and they help to control the number of red cells. For example, on a day when the skin loses 600 mL of water and urine 1500 mL, a rise of the skin loss to 1500 mL has to be matched by a fall of urine volume, which ADH brings about.

An enzyme released by the JG cells when the GFR or blood pressure falls; it starts the formation of angiotensin II.
A hormone of the adrenal cortex that makes the DCT reabsorb Na⁺ and water.

sections.heading: 4. Other excretory organs, disorders, haemodialysis and kidney transplant
sections.body_md:
**Other excretory organs.** The **lungs** remove about 200 mL of **CO₂** a minute and also water vapour. The **liver** secretes **bilirubin and biliverdin**, **cholesterol**, **degraded steroid hormones**, vitamins and drugs into the bile, and they leave with the digestive wastes. The **skin**: **sweat glands** produce **sweat** (water, NaCl, small amounts of urea and lactic acid), mainly for cooling; **sebaceous glands** secrete **sebum** (sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes) that protects and lubricates the skin.

**Disorders.**
- **Uraemia:** accumulation of **urea in the blood** because of kidney malfunction; it may lead to **renal failure**, in which the kidneys cannot filter the blood.
- **Renal calculi:** stones or **insoluble masses of crystallised salts (such as oxalates)** formed within the kidney.
- **Glomerulonephritis (nephritis):** **inflammation of the glomeruli** of the kidney.

**Haemodialysis.** Blood from a convenient artery (usually of the arm) is pumped into a **dialysing unit (artificial kidney)** after adding **heparin** (an anticoagulant). The unit has a coiled **cellophane tube** (a semipermeable membrane) surrounded by **dialysing fluid** with the same composition as plasma except that it has **no nitrogenous wastes**. Urea and other small molecules **diffuse out** of the blood into the fluid, down their concentration gradient, while blood cells and proteins stay in the tube. The cleaned blood is returned to a vein after **anti-heparin** is added. The dialysis has to be repeated, usually about three times a week.

**Kidney transplant.** The **ultimate method** in the correction of acute renal failure: a healthy kidney from a donor (preferably a close relative, to reduce the chance of **rejection** by the immune system) is placed in the patient, who takes drugs that suppress rejection. Books differ in detail on the numbers; the principle is what is asked.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the nitrogenous waste of an animal without relating it to the water available.
- Drawing the efferent arteriole wider than the afferent arteriole.
- Saying that proteins pass into the filtrate, or that the ascending limb is permeable to water.
- Mixing up the sources of the hormones (ADH from the neurohypophysis, aldosterone from the adrenal cortex, ANF from the heart, renin from the JG cells).
- Writing the renin-angiotensin steps out of order.
- Describing dialysis without the cellophane tube, the dialysing fluid with no nitrogenous wastes, or heparin.
- Confusing uraemia with glomerulonephritis.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, a location, a give-a-reason, a waste and its animal, a hormone and its source.
- 2–3-mark questions: modes of excretion, the three processes of urine formation, the counter-current mechanism, GFR calculations, ADH, the role of the skin, liver and lungs, dialysis.
- 5-mark questions in parts: labelled diagrams of a kidney L.S. or a nephron; urine formation with GFR; the counter-current mechanism with a diagram; regulation by ADH, RAAS and ANF; dialysis and transplant.

cards.back_md: About one million.
Filtration of blood under pressure; only proteins and cells stay behind.

cards.front_md: Which part reabsorbs most of the filtrate?
cards.back_md: The PCT.
H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia.
Permeable to water, not to electrolytes; filtrate becomes concentrated.
Impermeable to water; salts leave; filtrate becomes dilute.
Fluid in two nearby tubes flowing in opposite directions.

cards.front_md: What does the JGA release when the GFR falls?
cards.back_md: Renin.

Makes the DCT reabsorb Na⁺ and water.

cards.back_md: Erythropoietin.

cards.back_md: To stop the blood from clotting in the unit.

questions.stem_md: The embryo of a bird develops inside a hard shell, which is closed to the outside until it hatches. Which nitrogenous waste does it produce, and why is that suitable?

options.text_md: Ammonia, because it is harmless and dissolves easily in the egg fluid
Urea, because it can be passed out through the shell as the egg warms
Uric acid, because it is almost insoluble and can be stored in the egg without poisoning the embryo
Ammonia, because the egg fluid can be changed every day

questions.solution_md: Uric acid is the least toxic waste and needs almost no water, so it can be stored as crystals in the sealed egg — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A lungfish excretes mostly ammonia while it lives in a river, but when the river dries up and it lies in a mud burrow it excretes mostly urea. What is the advantage of this change?

options.text_md: Urea is more toxic than ammonia, so it can be stored without being absorbed
Urea is made from carbon dioxide and so gives the fish energy
Urea needs more water than ammonia and so keeps the burrow moist
Urea is less toxic than ammonia and needs much less water, so it can be kept in the body until the rain returns

questions.solution_md: In a dry burrow there is no water to flush out toxic ammonia, so it is converted to the less toxic urea — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following animals excretes its nitrogenous waste mainly as uric acid?

options.text_md: Goldfish
Rabbit
Tadpole of a frog
Cockroach

questions.solution_md: Insects, birds and reptiles are uricotelic; the fish and the tadpole excrete ammonia and the rabbit urea — option (d).

questions.stem_md: One kidney has 1,100,000 nephrons, of which 15 percent are juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops of Henle. How many juxtamedullary nephrons does that kidney have?
Give a reason: Birds can conserve water by excreting uric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Uric acid is **almost insoluble and non-toxic**, so it is passed out as a **paste with very little water**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between ammonotelism and uricotelism with reference to the waste, the water needed and one animal of each kind.

answer.model_answer_md: In **ammonotelism** the waste is **ammonia**, which is very toxic and needs **a large amount of water** to remove it, as in **bony fishes**. In **uricotelism** the waste is **uric acid**, which is almost insoluble and needs **very little water**, as in **birds or reptiles**.

questions.solution_md: Waste, water and example for each.

marking_scheme.step: Uricotelism: uric acid, little water, example

questions.stem_md: State one structural difference between the cortex and the medulla of the kidney, and name the extensions of the cortex between the pyramids.

answer.model_answer_md: The **cortex** is the outer region that contains the **Malpighian bodies and convoluted tubules**, while the **medulla** is the inner region made of cone-shaped **renal pyramids** with the loops of Henle and collecting ducts. The extensions of the cortex between the pyramids are the **renal columns**.

questions.solution_md: Cortex against medulla; renal columns.

questions.stem_md: Arrange ammonia, urea and uric acid in order of increasing toxicity, and relate each to the habitat of an animal that excretes it.

answer.model_answer_md: The order of increasing toxicity is **uric acid, then urea, then ammonia**. **Ammonia**, the most toxic, needs plenty of water to flush it out, so it is excreted by **aquatic animals such as bony fishes**. **Urea**, moderately toxic, is excreted by **mammals and land amphibians**, which can spare some water. **Uric acid** needs almost no water and is excreted by animals that must save it, such as **birds and desert reptiles**.

questions.solution_md: Order of toxicity; each waste with its habitat.

marking_scheme.step: Urea and uric acid with their habitats

questions.stem_md: Trace the path of blood through the kidney from the afferent arteriole to the renal vein, naming the capillaries that it passes, and state why the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole.

answer.model_answer_md: Blood enters the **glomerulus** through the **afferent arteriole**, leaves it by the **efferent arteriole**, then flows through the **peritubular capillaries** around the tubule (and the **vasa recta** in juxtamedullary nephrons) and is collected into veins and the **renal vein**. The efferent arteriole is **narrower** so that the **blood pressure in the glomerulus stays high**, which drives ultrafiltration.

questions.solution_md: Path of blood; narrow efferent arteriole.

marking_scheme.step: Afferent arteriole, glomerulus and efferent arteriole
Peritubular capillaries or vasa recta and the renal vein
Narrow efferent arteriole keeps the pressure high

(b) Describe the structure of a Malpighian body. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The diagram shows the **Bowman’s capsule** around the **glomerulus** with the wide **afferent arteriole** and narrow **efferent arteriole**; the coiled **PCT**; the **loop of Henle** with a **descending** and an **ascending limb** dipping into the medulla; the coiled **DCT**; the **collecting duct**; and the **peritubular capillaries** and **vasa recta**. The cortex and medulla are marked.

(b) The **Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)** consists of the **glomerulus**, a tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole, and the **Bowman’s capsule**, a double-walled cup of epithelial cells that surrounds it. The efferent arteriole carries blood away.

questions.stem_md: A thin sample of fluid is taken from the hairpin bend at the bottom of a long loop of Henle in the inner medulla. The osmolarity of the tissue fluid there is about 1200 mOsmol per L. The filtrate in the loop at that point has an osmolarity closest to

options.text_md: 300 mOsmol per L
600 mOsmol per L
100 mOsmol per L
1200 mOsmol per L

questions.solution_md: Water leaves the descending limb until the filtrate matches the surrounding fluid, so it is most concentrated at the bend: 1200 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The glomerular blood pressure of a patient in shock falls to 45 mm Hg. The pressure in the capsule is 18 mm Hg and the osmotic pressure of the blood is 32 mm Hg. What happens to filtration?

options.text_md: Filtration increases, because the capsule pressure is low
Filtration continues unchanged, because the osmotic pressure is high
Filtration stops, because the opposing pressures (50 mm Hg) exceed the glomerular pressure
Filtration continues at half its rate, because the pressure is divided between the capsule and the blood

questions.solution_md: Net pressure $= 45 - (18 + 32) = -5$ mm Hg, which is negative, so no filtration occurs — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A routine urine test of a boy shows plasma proteins in his urine, although he has no other symptoms. Which structure is most likely to be damaged?

options.text_md: The loop of Henle
The urethra
The ureter
The filtration membrane between the glomerular capillaries and the Bowman’s capsule

questions.solution_md: Proteins are too large to pass through the healthy filtration membrane; if they appear in the urine, the membrane must be damaged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: After a long period without food, a person’s urine is found to be more acidic than usual. Which process of urine formation has increased?

options.text_md: Ultrafiltration of plasma proteins
Tubular secretion of hydrogen ions into the filtrate
Reabsorption of glucose in the PCT
Reabsorption of water in the descending limb

questions.solution_md: Tubule cells secrete H⁺ into the filtrate, which helps to maintain the pH of the blood and makes urine acid — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The flow of filtrate in the two limbs of the loop of Henle is called counter-current flow because

options.text_md: the filtrate moves against the flow of blood in the renal vein
the flow stops and starts at regular intervals
the filtrate moves in opposite directions in the two limbs, which lie close together
both limbs carry the filtrate in the same direction at different speeds

questions.solution_md: Counter-current means flow in opposite directions in adjacent tubes — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a juxtamedullary nephron, the hairpin-shaped blood vessels that run alongside the loop of Henle also carry their blood in opposite directions. What is their main function in the concentration of urine?

options.text_md: They remove the extra water from the medulla without washing away the salt that maintains the gradient
They filter the plasma proteins out of the blood
They secrete renin into the medulla
They store urine until it can be passed

questions.solution_md: The vasa recta remove water but return the NaCl, so the medullary gradient is kept — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
A student measures three fluids from a healthy person and records their contents in g per 100 mL.

| Fluid | Protein | Glucose | Urea |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 7 | 0.1 | 0.03 |
| Y | 0 | 0.1 | 0.03 |
| Z | 0 | 0 | 2 |

Which row correctly identifies the three fluids?

options.text_md: X is plasma, Y is glomerular filtrate and Z is urine
X is urine, Y is plasma and Z is glomerular filtrate
X is glomerular filtrate, Y is urine and Z is plasma
X is plasma, Y is urine and Z is glomerular filtrate

questions.solution_md: Only plasma has proteins; the filtrate is like plasma without proteins; urine has no glucose (reabsorbed) and a high urea concentration (water reabsorbed) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A drug stops the transport of salts out of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. What is the likely effect on the urine?

options.text_md: The medullary gradient falls, so the urine becomes more dilute and larger in volume
The medullary gradient rises, so the urine becomes more concentrated
The GFR rises to twice its value
The urine contains more protein

questions.solution_md: Without salt leaving the ascending limb, the osmolarity gradient of the medulla cannot be kept, so less water can be reabsorbed from the collecting duct — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The GFR of a person is 125 mL per minute, and the PCT reabsorbs 70 percent of the filtrate. How many mL of filtrate pass into the loop of Henle each minute?
questions.solution_md: Reabsorbed in the PCT $= 70/100 \times 125 = 87.5$ mL; left $= 125 - 87.5 = 37.5$ mL per minute.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have a brush border of microvilli.

**Reason (R):** The brush border increases the surface area for reabsorption.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the larger surface explains the large amount of reabsorption in the PCT — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The ascending limb is impermeable to water, although it lets electrolytes out, so the filtrate becomes dilute.

questions.stem_md: Almost every constituent of plasma passes into the Bowman’s capsule except blood cells and ______.
questions.solution_md: Plasma proteins.

questions.stem_md: A kidney disease reduces a patient’s glomerular filtration rate to 80 mL per minute. How many litres of filtrate do her kidneys form in a day? Give one decimal place.
A man’s glomerular filtration rate is 110 mL per minute and he passes 1.8 L of urine in a day. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed? Give one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: Filtrate $= 110 \times 1440/1000 = 158.4$ L; reabsorbed $= 158.4 - 1.8 = 156.6$ L; $156.6/158.4 \times 100 = 98.86$, or 98.9 percent to one decimal place.

questions.stem_md: In an athlete the glomerular blood pressure is 66 mm Hg, the pressure in the capsule is 15 mm Hg and the osmotic pressure of the blood is 28 mm Hg. Calculate the net filtration pressure in mm Hg.

The osmolarity of the glomerular filtrate is 300 mOsmol per L. A man who has not drunk for a while forms urine with an osmolarity of 840 mOsmol per L. How many times more concentrated than the filtrate is his urine? Give one decimal place.
Name the three processes of urine formation in the order in which they occur, and name the site of the first.

answer.model_answer_md: The processes are **glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration)**, **selective reabsorption** and **tubular secretion**. Ultrafiltration takes place at the **glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule**.

questions.solution_md: Three processes; site of the first.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by counter-current flow? Name the two structures of a juxtamedullary nephron in which it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Counter-current flow** is the flow of fluid in **opposite directions** in two tubes lying close together. It occurs in the **two limbs of the loop of Henle** (the filtrate) and in the **two limbs of the vasa recta** (the blood).

questions.solution_md: Opposite flow; loop of Henle and vasa recta.

marking_scheme.step: Flow in opposite directions in neighbouring tubes
Loop of Henle and vasa recta

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The filtrate becomes more concentrated as it flows down the descending limb of the loop of Henle.

answer.model_answer_md: The descending limb is **permeable to water**, which **leaves the filtrate** into the more concentrated tissue fluid, while electrolytes cannot easily enter or leave.

questions.solution_md: Water leaves.

marking_scheme.step: Water leaves because the limb is permeable to it

questions.stem_md: Define glomerular filtration rate (GFR). A person has a GFR of 110 mL per minute and passes 1.8 L of urine in a day. Calculate the filtrate formed in a day and explain why the volume of urine is so much smaller.

answer.model_answer_md: The **GFR** is the **volume of filtrate formed by the kidneys each minute**. The filtrate formed in a day is $110 \times 1440/1000 = 158.4$ L. Only 1.8 L is passed because the remaining $156.6$ L (about 98.9 percent) is **reabsorbed into the blood** by the tubules, mostly in the **PCT**, which takes back useful substances and most of the water.

questions.solution_md: Definition; daily filtrate; reabsorption.

marking_scheme.step: Most is reabsorbed by the tubules

questions.stem_md: Follow a drop of filtrate down the descending limb, up the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and through the collecting duct. State what happens to its concentration at each stage.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **descending limb**, which is **permeable to water**, water leaves, so the filtrate becomes **more concentrated**. In the **ascending limb**, which is **impermeable to water**, electrolytes are transported out, so the filtrate becomes **dilute**. In the **collecting duct**, which passes through the concentrated medulla, **water is reabsorbed** and the filtrate becomes **concentrated urine**.

questions.solution_md: Concentrated; dilute; concentrated again.

marking_scheme.step: Collecting duct: water reabsorbed, concentrated urine

questions.stem_md: What is tubular secretion? Name three substances that are secreted and state two ways in which it helps the body.

answer.model_answer_md: **Tubular secretion** is the **passage of substances from the blood into the filtrate** through the cells of the tubule, mainly in the **PCT and DCT**. The substances are **hydrogen ions, potassium ions and ammonia**. It helps to maintain the **pH** and the **ionic balance** of the blood, and removes extra waste.

questions.solution_md: Definition; three substances; two benefits.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the three processes by which urine is formed, naming where each takes place. [3]
(b) A person’s GFR is 110 mL per minute. What is the volume of filtrate formed in a day, and why is only about 1.8 L passed as urine? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Ultrafiltration** takes place at the **glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule**, where blood pressure forces water and small solutes, but not proteins and cells, through the filtration membrane. **Selective reabsorption** takes place mostly in the **PCT**, which returns glucose, amino acids, salts and water to the blood; the loop, DCT and collecting duct reabsorb more water. **Tubular secretion** in the **PCT and DCT** adds H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia to the filtrate.

(b) Filtrate $= 110 \times 1440/1000 = 158.4$ L a day. About 98.9 percent is **reabsorbed into the blood**, leaving only a small volume as urine.

questions.solution_md: Three processes with sites; daily filtrate.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the loop of Henle and the vasa recta, showing the direction of flow and the gradient of osmolarity of the medulla. [2]
(b) Explain how the counter-current mechanism enables the kidney to produce urine more concentrated than the filtrate. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The diagram shows the **descending and ascending limbs** with arrows in **opposite directions**, the **vasa recta** alongside in opposite directions, the **collecting duct**, and the osmolarity rising from **300 mOsmol per L in the cortex to 1200 in the inner medulla**.

(b) The **ascending limb** passes out NaCl, and the **descending limb** loses water; the **vasa recta** take away the extra water but pick up and return the NaCl and urea. These exchanges keep a **steep gradient of osmolarity** in the medulla. The **collecting duct** passes through this gradient and **loses water**, so urine becomes up to **four times as concentrated** as the filtrate.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; explanation.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Limbs and vasa recta with directions
(b) Ascending limb salts and descending limb water
(b) Collecting duct loses water: concentrated urine

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A clinic estimated the glomerular filtration rate of a man from his creatinine clearance, GFR $=$ U × V / P, where U is the creatinine concentration in the urine, V the urine flow and P the concentration in the plasma. Creatinine is filtered but not reabsorbed.

| | Before the illness | After the illness |
|---|---|---|
| Urine creatinine, U (mg per mL) | 0.6 | 0.6 |
| Urine flow, V (mL per minute) | 1.5 | 1.5 |
| Plasma creatinine, P (mg per mL) | 0.012 | 0.03 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 75 mL per minute

**(b)** (a) The GFR has fallen to 30 mL per minute, so the kidneys are filtering less blood

**(c)** (i) The fall is $(75 - 30)/75 \times 100 = 60$ percent. **Urea** is likely to accumulate in the blood, a condition called **uraemia**.

**OR** (ii) With a very low GFR the kidneys cannot remove **urea and other wastes**, which build up and poison the body. **Haemodialysis** removes them from the blood artificially, and a **transplant** provides a kidney that filters normally.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $0.6 \times 1.5 / 0.012 = 75$ mL per minute.

**(b)** GFR $= 0.6 \times 1.5 / 0.03 = 30$ mL per minute, lower than before: wastes accumulate in the plasma — option (a).

**(c)** (i) 60 percent; urea.

(ii) Wastes build up; dialysis or a transplant.

children.stem_md: Calculate the man’s GFR before the illness, in mL per minute.
After the illness the plasma creatinine rises to 0.03 mg per mL while the urine values are unchanged. What does this show?

options.text_md: The GFR has fallen to 30 mL per minute, so the kidneys are filtering less blood
The GFR has risen, so the kidneys are filtering more blood
The tubules are reabsorbing more creatinine
The GFR is unchanged, because the urine flow is unchanged

children.solution_md: GFR $= 0.6 \times 1.5 / 0.03 = 30$ mL per minute, lower than before: wastes accumulate in the plasma — option (a).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): By what percentage has the GFR fallen, and which substance, besides creatinine, is likely to accumulate in his blood?

answer.model_answer_md: The fall is $(75 - 30)/75 \times 100 = 60$ percent. **Urea** is likely to accumulate in the blood, a condition called **uraemia**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why must a patient with a much-reduced GFR be treated by haemodialysis or a transplant if the kidney does not recover?

answer.model_answer_md: With a very low GFR the kidneys cannot remove **urea and other wastes**, which build up and poison the body. **Haemodialysis** removes them from the blood artificially, and a **transplant** provides a kidney that filters normally.

alternatives.solution_md: Wastes build up; dialysis or a transplant.

marking_scheme.step: Wastes accumulate when the GFR is low
Dialysis or transplant replaces kidney function

questions.stem_md: A patient with damage to the pituitary gland passes about 12 litres of very dilute urine a day and is always thirsty. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text_md: Without ADH, the glomerular filtration rate falls to zero
Too much aldosterone is making the PCT reabsorb all the water
Without ADH, the distal tubule and collecting duct do not reabsorb enough water
The loop of Henle has become permeable to proteins

questions.solution_md: ADH makes the last parts of the tubule permeable to water; without it water stays in the urine — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A drug blocks the enzyme that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II in a patient with high blood pressure. What is the expected effect?

options.text_md: The blood pressure rises, because more renin is released
The blood pressure falls, because there is less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone
There is no effect, because angiotensin I has the same action
The filtration rate rises, because the afferent arteriole narrows

questions.solution_md: Angiotensin II constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone, so blocking its formation lowers the pressure — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A cricketer trains for a month in a mountain village at a high altitude, and his red blood cell count rises. Which hormone released by the kidney was responsible?

options.text_md: Erythropoietin
Aldosterone
Atrial natriuretic factor
Antidiuretic hormone

questions.solution_md: The kidney releases erythropoietin when oxygen is short, and it stimulates the bone marrow to make red cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A healthy adult can delay passing urine for a time after the bladder is full, but a young baby cannot. What is the main reason?

options.text_md: The adult’s kidneys stop forming urine until a toilet is found
The adult’s bladder does not have stretch receptors
The adult can voluntarily control the urethral sphincter through the nervous system
The adult’s ureters can hold urine for hours

questions.solution_md: The micturition reflex involves stretch receptors and the CNS, and in adults the sphincter can be controlled voluntarily — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a homeostatic function of the kidneys?

options.text_md: Regulating the osmolarity of body fluids
Helping to maintain the pH of the blood
Helping to regulate the blood pressure
Digestion of fats in the small intestine

questions.solution_md: The kidneys regulate fluid volume, ions, pH and blood pressure, but fat digestion is done by bile and lipases — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The juxtaglomerular (JG) cells that release renin are modified cells of the

options.text_md: proximal convoluted tubule
afferent arteriole
loop of Henle
collecting duct

questions.solution_md: JG cells are modified cells of the afferent arteriole, next to the macula densa of the DCT — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Aldosterone helps to raise the blood pressure.

**Reason (R):** Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal medulla.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: aldosterone makes the DCT reabsorb Na⁺ and water. R is false: it is secreted by the adrenal cortex — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? ADH is released by the neurohypophysis when the osmolarity of the body fluids falls.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. ADH is released when the osmolarity rises (or the volume falls) and increases water reabsorption.

questions.stem_md: ANF stands for atrial ______ factor, a hormone from the heart that lowers blood pressure.
questions.solution_md: Natriuretic.

questions.stem_md: On a cold day a person takes in 2500 mL of water and loses 300 mL through the skin, 300 mL through the lungs and 100 mL with the faeces. How many mL of urine must she form to keep her water balance?
A traveller walks through a desert for several hours and sweats heavily. What happens to the volume and concentration of her urine, and why?

options.text_md: More urine, more dilute, because ADH is released when water is lost
Less urine, more concentrated, because ADH makes the tubule reabsorb more water
The same volume and concentration, because sweat is made from urine
No urine at all, because the glomerular filtration stops

questions.solution_md: Water loss raises the osmolarity of the blood, ADH is released, and the kidney conserves water — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A boy eats a very salty meal. Explain how his body responds so that the osmolarity of his body fluids is brought back to normal.

answer.model_answer_md: The salt raises the **osmolarity of the blood**. **Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus** detect it, and the **neurohypophysis releases ADH**, so the **DCT and collecting duct reabsorb more water** and he passes less, more concentrated urine; he also feels thirsty and drinks.

questions.solution_md: Osmoreceptors; ADH; more water reabsorbed.

marking_scheme.step: Rise in osmolarity detected; ADH released
More water reabsorbed and a concentrated urine

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A person who has lost a lot of blood secretes more aldosterone.

answer.model_answer_md: The fall in blood pressure and GFR makes the **JG cells release renin**, which leads to **angiotensin II**, and this stimulates the **adrenal cortex** to release aldosterone.

questions.solution_md: Renin system activated.

marking_scheme.step: Fall in pressure activates renin and angiotensin II, which stimulates aldosterone

questions.stem_md: Name the part of the brain that detects a rise in the osmolarity of the blood and the gland that releases ADH. State the effect of ADH on the tubule.

answer.model_answer_md: **Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus** detect the rise, and the **neurohypophysis** releases **ADH**. ADH makes the **distal parts of the tubule more permeable to water**, so more water is reabsorbed.

questions.solution_md: Hypothalamus; neurohypophysis; more water reabsorbed.

marking_scheme.step: More water reabsorbed in the distal tubule

questions.stem_md: Name the hormone secreted by the kidney that controls the formation of red blood cells, and state the condition that stimulates its release.

answer.model_answer_md: The hormone is **erythropoietin**. Its release is stimulated by **low oxygen (hypoxia) in the blood reaching the kidney**, and it acts on the **bone marrow** to make **more red blood cells**.

questions.solution_md: Erythropoietin; hypoxia.

marking_scheme.step: Stimulus: low oxygen; action on the bone marrow

questions.stem_md: Micturition is a reflex but an adult can control it. Describe the reflex in two steps and say what makes the voluntary control possible.

answer.model_answer_md: When the bladder fills, **stretch receptors** in its wall send signals to the **CNS**, which sends **motor messages** that make the **bladder muscle contract and the sphincter relax**, so urine is passed. The **urethral sphincter is under voluntary control**, so an adult can delay it.

questions.solution_md: Receptors; CNS; muscle and sphincter; voluntary sphincter.

marking_scheme.step: Stretch receptors signal the CNS; motor messages cause the bladder to contract and the sphincter to relax

questions.stem_md: State the source of ANF, the condition that causes its release and its effects, and explain why it is called a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

answer.model_answer_md: **ANF** (atrial natriuretic factor) is released by the **atrial walls of the heart** when the **blood volume and pressure rise**. It causes **vasodilation** and a fall in blood pressure. This is the **opposite** of angiotensin II, which constricts the vessels and raises the pressure, so ANF acts as a **check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism**.

questions.solution_md: Source and stimulus; effect; opposes the RAAS.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain how ADH regulates the water balance of the body, naming the sensors and the gland concerned. [2]
(b) Describe the sequence of events of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism when the glomerular blood pressure falls. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus** detect a rise in the osmolarity of the body fluids and the **neurohypophysis** releases **ADH**. It makes the **DCT and collecting duct reabsorb more water**, so less, more concentrated urine is formed; when the volume has risen, the release stops.

(b) The fall activates the **JG cells** to release **renin**, which converts **angiotensinogen** to **angiotensin I** and then to **angiotensin II**. Angiotensin II is a **vasoconstrictor**, which raises the glomerular pressure and the GFR, and it stimulates the **adrenal cortex** to release **aldosterone**, which makes the **DCT reabsorb Na⁺ and water**, raising the blood pressure.

questions.solution_md: ADH regulation; RAAS sequence.

marking_scheme.step: (b) JG cells release renin; angiotensin I to II

questions.stem_md: During haemodialysis the glucose of a patient’s blood is not lost into the dialysing fluid. This is because the dialysing fluid

options.text_md: has the same concentration of glucose as the plasma, so there is no gradient for it
contains no water, so glucose cannot dissolve in it
is separated from the blood by a membrane that lets only urea through
is warmer than the blood and so stops diffusion

questions.solution_md: The fluid has the composition of plasma except for the nitrogenous wastes, so only the wastes move down a gradient — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A kidney transplanted from an unrelated donor works well for a few days and then fails. The most likely reason is that the

options.text_md: new kidney was too large for the abdomen
immune system of the patient recognised the new kidney as foreign and attacked it
patient’s blood group changed after the operation
new kidney could not be supplied with oxygen by the renal artery

questions.solution_md: Rejection by the recipient’s immune system is the main problem of a transplant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which glands of the skin release sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes that protect and lubricate the skin?

options.text_md: Sebaceous glands
Sweat glands
Salivary glands

questions.stem_md: Give three points of comparison between haemodialysis and a kidney transplant as treatments of renal failure.

Dialysis replaces only the **filtering**, but a transplant also restores the **hormonal functions**. The main risk of a transplant is **rejection** by the immune system, so a **close relative** is preferred as the donor and drugs are given.

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) **Heparin** is an anticoagulant: it **prevents the blood from clotting** in the unit.

(c) A transplanted kidney does **all the work of a kidney** and does not need to be repeated every few days.
